title: There is an unborn
hookLine: there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade; were there not, there'd be no escape
carry: because there is, an escape is known

cards: Everything you've ever touched was born, or made, or put together. Your phone. Your house.
Your body. Your mood this morning. Every one of them came from causes, and every one will come apart.
That raises a hard question. If everything is made, and everything comes apart, is there anything at all that isn't? Is there a way out of the making?
In the eighth and last chapter of the Udana, the Buddha answers with four words that start with un.

teach.b: The setting is a talk on nibbana to the monks. Here's the saying, paraphrased closely.
There is, monks, an unborn, an unbecome, an unmade, an unconditioned.

teach.h: IF THERE WERE NOT, NO ESCAPE.
teach.b: If there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, no escape would be known from the born, the become, the made, the conditioned. But because there is, an escape is known.
Notice where the weight falls: on two small words, there is. Not it might be, not we hope. The text doesn't describe the unborn at all.
It argues for it, from the escape: if there were only the made, there'd be no way out of it. How do traditions read it?
Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as nibbana itself: not a self, not a soul, not a creator, but the unconditioned. Other schools have drawn on the passage in their own ways.
The text itself simply says, there is. Look back at the week. Nanda's pull home.
Meghiya not yet ripe. The elephant read whole. Moths at the lamp.
Suppavasa giving. Visakha's hundred sorrows. Every one was about the born and the made.
Today, the Udana points past them.

how: The saying on the unborn is studied in Theravada teaching on nibbana and is quoted by teachers of many Buddhist schools; it also appears in the Itivuttaka (Iti 43).

o: a child who is not yet born
a soul that is never born

games.q: there is an unborn: tap the pairs.

s: the saying describes the unborn in detail
every word is a negative; it says what it isn't, and that it is.
the saying argues from the possibility of escape
if there were no unborn, no escape from the born would be known.
Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as a creator god
they generally read it as nibbana, the unconditioned, not a self or a creator.

games.q: you're a monk at the Buddha's talk on nibbana. you ask: if everything is made and comes apart, how can there be a way out? what does the saying answer?
o: there is no way out; accept it.
there is an unborn, unmade; because there is, there is an escape.
the way out is to be reborn in heaven.
games.why: the Udana says there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, and that because there is, escape from the made is known.

practice: Notice how everything in your experience is moving: the breath, sounds, sensations, thoughts arriving and leaving. Don't chase any of them, and don't try to find the unborn either; it isn't a thing to find.
Let the movement go on, and rest as the quiet that notices it.

wordCard.voice: Ajāta. Unborn: one of four words, with unbecome, unmade and unconditioned, that the Udana uses for nibbana, the escape from everything made.

orig.note: Pali ajata: unborn. the saying begins atthi bhikkhave ajatam: there is, monks, an unborn.

carryVoice: Your line: because there is, an escape is known. A week of the born and the made, and one saying that points past them. That's a week.
